title: Iteration and Approximate Solutions
standard_text: Find approximate solutions to equations numerically using iteration; use a change of sign to locate a root.
meta_desc: Free Year 11 GCSE maths worksheets on iteration: using iteration formulae, rearranging equations, change of sign and finding solutions to 2 decimal places. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Put each answer back into the formula to get the next one.
key_sub: A change of sign shows a solution in between.
body_html:
How it works

An iteration formula such as xn+1 = ∛(2xn + 5) is made by rearranging an equation (here x³ − 2x − 5 = 0). Start with x0, work out x1, put it back in to get x2, and so on. Use the ANS key on a calculator.

If f(a) and f(b) have different signs, there is a solution of f(x) = 0 between a and b.

Example

xn+1 = √(3xn + 4), x0 = 1. Find x1.

√(3 × 1 + 4) = √7

Answer: 2.646

Example

f(x) = x³ − 4x − 2. Show there is a root between 2 and 3.

f(2) = −2

f(3) = 13

Answer: The sign changes, so there is a root between 2 and 3

Common mistakes

  • Using x₀ again instead of the new value.
  • Rounding too early.
  • Changing a sign when rearranging the equation.

faq.a: A rule that turns one approximation into the next, such as x(n+1) = ∛(2x(n) + 5). The values get closer and closer to a solution.

faq.q: How does a change of sign show a solution?
faq.a: If f(a) is negative and f(b) is positive (or the other way), the graph crosses the x-axis between a and b, so f(x) = 0 has a solution there.
